CHAPTER 11
Advanced EC2 Administration
Versioned fleets, secure bootstrapping, placement, capacity, and lifecycle operations
VOLUME 6B | CHAPTER 11
Learning Objectives

Use launch templates as versioned instance specifications.

Require IMDSv2 and use instance profiles instead of stored credentials.

Select placement, capacity, hibernation, and purchase options correctly.

Operate immutable fleets and troubleshoot launch or readiness failures.
11.1 From servers to replaceable fleets
A manually configured instance is an operational exception: it is difficult to reproduce, audit, patch, and
recover. Production teams define EC2 capacity through approved AMIs, launch templates, instance roles,
network policy, observability, health checks, and replacement rules. Persistent state is externalized so
unhealthy or noncompliant instances can be replaced instead of repaired indefinitely. The fleet definition belongs in version control and a delivery pipeline. A change is tested as a new image
or launch-template version, deployed to a limited scope, observed, and then promoted. This separates an
approved release from the latest change and creates a practical rollback path.
11.2 Launch templates and image strategy
Launch templates store launch parameters including AMI, type, storage, security groups, instance profile,
metadata options, user data, monitoring, placement, and tags. Versions support audit and rollback. Production Auto Scaling groups should consume an explicitly approved version or a controlled promotion
mechanism. Most mature platforms use a hybrid image strategy. Stable operating-system packages, security agents,
runtimes, and baseline configuration are baked into a golden AMI. Environment-specific values are
applied during launch.

11.3 IMDSv2 and instance identity
The Instance Metadata Service exposes instance identity and temporary credentials for the attached role. IMDSv2 uses a token-based session flow and should normally be required in the launch template. Disable
the endpoint when it is unnecessary, use a low hop limit unless a documented container path requires
more, and never persist temporary metadata credentials. Applications should use current AWS SDK credential providers rather than calling metadata directly. Requiring IMDSv2 can expose old applications or agents that still use IMDSv1, so enforcement should
include inventory, testing, and remediation.

11.4 Nitro, placement, capacity, and lifecycle
Modern EC2 families are commonly based on the Nitro System, which offloads networking, EBS,
management, and isolation functions. Engineers should confirm that the chosen family supports required
capabilities such as enhanced networking, high EBS bandwidth, hibernation, enclaves, bare metal, or
Multi-Attach scenarios. Cluster placement optimizes tightly coupled communication in one Availability Zone; partition placement
separates distributed-system groups across partitions; spread placement separates a limited number of
critical instances. None replaces multi-AZ resilience. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances primarily
address cost, Capacity Reservations address matching zonal capacity, and Spot provides interruptible
spare capacity. Reboot restarts the guest. Stop/start releases compute and may move the instance. Hibernation writes
memory to an encrypted root volume and stops, subject to support constraints. Termination removes the
instance and volumes marked for deletion. Immutable fleets normally replace rather than preserve failed

CHAPTER 12
Advanced Amazon VPC
Address planning, subnet tiers, routing, egress, endpoints, IPv6, and hybrid-ready networks
VOLUME 6B | CHAPTER 12
Learning Objectives

Create non-overlapping IPv4/IPv6 address plans.

Design public, private, and isolated subnets across Availability Zones.

Choose internet, NAT, endpoint, peering, and Transit Gateway paths.

Troubleshoot complete forward and return routes.
12.1 VPC as a routing and ownership boundary
A VPC is a regional virtual network containing address ranges, subnets, route tables, gateways, endpoints,
security controls, and connectivity. Subnets are Availability Zone resources. Good design begins with
failure domains and required communications, not with the default wizard. CIDR allocation must account for growth, containers, managed-service interfaces, future environments,
hybrid networks, acquisitions, and regional expansion. Overlap makes peering, Transit Gateway, VPN, and
Direct Connect routing difficult or impossible. Reserve space and use a governed IP address management
process.
12.2 Subnet tiers and route evaluation
A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway; an IPv4 workload also needs a public address and
security permission. A private subnet can initiate internet connections through NAT without accepting
unsolicited inbound IPv4 sessions. An isolated subnet has no default internet route and uses only explicit
private routes and endpoints. AWS route selection uses longest-prefix match. A specific endpoint, peering, Transit Gateway, or appliance
route overrides a broader default route.

private routes and endpoints. AWS route selection uses longest-prefix match. A specific endpoint, peering, Transit Gateway, or appliance
route overrides a broader default route. Troubleshooting should write the source, destination, protocol,
forward route, policy checks, and return route before changing anything.
12.3 NAT, endpoints, and IPv6
A public NAT gateway resides in a public subnet and uses an Elastic IP. For zonal resilience, route each
private subnet to a NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone. One centralized NAT can reduce resource
count but creates a zonal dependency and cross-AZ data paths. NAT gateways have hourly and processing
costs and do not accept security groups. Gateway endpoints provide private route-table access to supported services such as S3 and DynamoDB. Interface endpoints create private network interfaces protected by security groups and are powered by
PrivateLink. Endpoint policies restrict the endpoint path but do not replace IAM or resource policies. IPv6 does not use NAT for address conservation. Dual-stack security must include IPv6 routes, security
rules, logs, DNS, and tooling. Use an egress-only internet gateway for outbound-only IPv6 internet
communication.

12.4 Multi-VPC, hybrid, and observability
VPC peering is simple point-to-point and non-transitive. Transit Gateway provides hub-and-spoke routing
at scale. PrivateLink exposes a service privately without broad network reachability. VPN provides
encrypted connectivity over the internet; Direct Connect supports dedicated private connectivity options. Every design must align routes on both sides and include DNS. Enable VPC Flow Logs at a useful scope, centralize retention, and monitor rejected flows, NAT behavior,
endpoint usage, IP exhaustion, and route changes. Reachability Analyzer evaluates configuration paths
but does not prove that an application is listening. VPC Block Public Access can provide authoritative
account-level guardrails where compatible with the architecture. VPC connectivity matrix

13.1 Multiple enforcement layers
A packet may be affected by routing, security groups, network ACLs, load-balancer listeners, endpoint
policies, appliance rules, host firewalls, and application authorization. Assign each layer a purpose instead
of duplicating every rule. Least privilege defines the required source, destination, protocol, and port; a
rule created only to make a test pass is technical debt.
13.2 Stateful security groups
Security groups attach to network interfaces, contain allow rules, and are stateful: return traffic for an
allowed connection is recognized without a reverse rule. They have no explicit deny. The preferred
pattern is client to ALB on HTTPS, ALB security group to application port, and application security group
to database port. A referenced security group identifies associated private interfaces for supported flows; it does not create
routing and is not group nesting. References are more stable than hard-coded addresses and clearly
express workload relationships.
13.3 Stateless network ACLs
NACLs associate with subnets and evaluate ordered inbound and outbound allow/deny rules. Because they
are stateless, request and return traffic, including client ephemeral ports, must be allowed. Complex
NACLs often create outages.

are stateless, request and return traffic, including client ephemeral ports, must be allowed. Complex
NACLs often create outages. Use them for coarse subnet guardrails or known denies while security groups
carry workload-specific policy.

13.4 Administrative access and egress
Public SSH/RDP should normally be replaced by Systems Manager Session Manager, a private operations
network, Client VPN, or another controlled path. Session Manager still requires least-privilege IAM,
agent/connectivity health, encrypted log delivery, and break-glass procedures. Mature platforms reduce unrestricted outbound traffic with endpoints, security-group destinations,
managed prefix lists, proxies, DNS controls, and centralized inspection. Discover real dependencies
through logs before enforcing restrictions, and provide approved paths for time, certificate validation,
package repositories, monitoring, and incident tools.
13.5 Segmentation and Zero Trust
Microsegmentation reduces reachable paths but does not replace identity. A practical Zero Trust posture
combines small network blast radius with workload identities, service authentication, device/user context,
secrets management, continuous logging, and explicit authorization. Security control comparison

CHAPTER 14
Amazon Route 53 and DNS Engineering
Authoritative DNS, routing policies, health evaluation, private resolution, and safe change
operations
VOLUME 6B | CHAPTER 14
Learning Objectives

Explain recursive and authoritative DNS resolution.

Design public and private hosted zones with clear ownership.

Choose Route 53 routing policies for the actual resilience objective.

Use aliases, health checks, Resolver endpoints, and query evidence correctly.

Operate DNS changes with tested rollback.
14.1 DNS is a distributed control plane
Applications depend on DNS before they can reach a load balancer, API, database, or service endpoint. A
resolver follows delegation from the root to a top-level domain and then to authoritative name servers. Caches retain answers according to the record time to live, so a change is not globally instantaneous. Route 53 is both an authoritative DNS service and a routing control plane. Reliability requires control of
registration, delegation, hosted-zone records, certificates, health signals, query logging, and change
ownership. A correct record in the wrong hosted zone does nothing; a correct hosted zone without
registrar delegation is not authoritative.
14.2 Hosted zones, records, and aliases
A public hosted zone answers internet DNS queries. A private hosted zone answers only through
associated VPCs and supported hybrid resolution paths. Split-horizon DNS can intentionally return
different answers internally and externally, but identical names across several private zones can create
confusing precedence. Common records include A and AAAA for addresses, CNAME for canonical names, MX for mail, TXT for
verification and policy, and NS/SOA records for authority.

confusing precedence. Common records include A and AAAA for addresses, CNAME for canonical names, MX for mail, TXT for
verification and policy, and NS/SOA records for authority. Route 53 alias records can point the zone apex
or another name to selected AWS resources without the CNAME apex restriction. An alias target and a
traditional CNAME are not interchangeable.
14.3 Routing policies and health
Simple routing returns one record set. Weighted routing distributes answers by configured weights and is
useful for gradual release, experiments, or controlled migration. Latency routing chooses the configured
Region expected to give lower latency. Geolocation uses user location, geoproximity considers resource
location and bias, multivalue answers can return several healthy records, and failover routing selects
primary or secondary based on health.

DNS routing does not proxy traffic and does not guarantee that an exact percentage of requests follows
each answer because resolvers cache and aggregate queries. Health checks should test the customer-
relevant path where possible. Evaluate Target Health can inherit health from supported alias targets,
while explicit Route 53 health checks can monitor endpoints or calculated combinations.
14.4 Hybrid DNS with Route 53 Resolver
Inbound Resolver endpoints allow on-premises resolvers to query selected private AWS namespaces. Outbound endpoints and forwarding rules send specified domains from VPCs to external resolvers. Rules
can be shared across accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager. Endpoint security groups,
availability across subnets, resolver capacity, logging, and loop prevention are production concerns. Avoid forwarding a domain in a circle between AWS and on-premises DNS. Define one authoritative
owner for each namespace, document delegation and forwarding, and test resolution from every relevant
network segment.
14.5 Safe DNS change management
Lowering TTL shortly before a planned migration can reduce cache persistence, but only after the
previous higher TTL has expired. Changes should include prechecks, staged records, certificate validation,
health readiness, explicit observation windows, rollback records, and post-change verification from
multiple resolvers. DNSSEC can protect authenticity where required but adds key and delegation lifecycle
responsibilities.

16.1 Auto Scaling is a feedback-control system
An Auto Scaling group maintains desired capacity between minimum and maximum limits and replaces
unhealthy instances. Scaling adds or removes capacity in response to a signal. The system is stable only
when the metric represents demand, new capacity becomes useful within the assumed time, dependencies
can absorb growth, and scale-in does not remove needed work. High availability begins with subnets in multiple Availability Zones, a launch template, health evaluation,
and deterministic bootstrapping. Auto Scaling is not a substitute for application statelessness, database
capacity planning, queue design, or regional disaster recovery.
16.2 Scaling policy selection
Target tracking adjusts capacity to keep a metric near a target and is the normal starting point for
proportional workloads. Step scaling changes capacity based on alarm breach severity. Scheduled scaling
handles known business events, while predictive scaling forecasts recurring demand and can provision
ahead of it. Multiple policies can coexist, but their interactions must be understood.

readiness time for slow-start applications but add state, patching, and cost considerations.

17.1 EBS architecture and failure boundaries
Amazon Elastic Block Store provides durable block devices for EC2. A volume is created in one Availability
Zone and attaches to compatible instances in that zone. The guest operating system creates partitions, file
systems, volume managers, databases, and application-level consistency on top of the device. EBS
durability does not eliminate corruption, accidental deletion, ransomware, or application-consistency
requirements. A resilient application should separate replaceable compute from persistent data, encrypt by default,
monitor performance, create recoverable points, and practice restore. Multi-AZ service availability usually
requires replication at the database or application layer, not an assumption that one EBS volume spans
zones.
17.2 Volume families and selection
General Purpose SSD gp3 is the normal starting point for boot volumes and many transactional workloads
because capacity, baseline performance, IOPS, and throughput can be adjusted independently within
service constraints. Provisioned IOPS SSD io2 is intended for latency-sensitive, I/O-intensive databases and
applications needing higher durability and predictable provisioned performance.

volumes created from encrypted snapshots. The KMS key policy, grants, account boundary, and lifecycle
become part of recoverability. Enabling encryption by default in each Region reduces unencrypted drift. Snapshots are incremental service-managed recovery points stored in Amazon S3 infrastructure, but they

blocks at a moment; application-consistent recovery may require flushing, freezing, database backup

needed when immediate full performance after restore matters.
